title: Pachanga era and records released too late
summary: Back from Japan, work slowed as charanga and pachanga rose; slow record releases made numbers old by the time they came out.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Ah-Ha, okay. Macho, you came back, the Pachanga was hot then. What did it do to the band?
Well, we was working, not as much as I would like to because the Charanga wasn't, you know, very popular and ....
(Second side of last tape (IV) -- pause - then)
.... collector's items.. You are not satisfied with that song?

Yes, it was good, very good. To me was one of the best recording that we had, but is possible that we was kind of late. Is like for instance, you try to record a disco now. It's kind of late. Sometimes you don't move as fast as you should.

And in many case too, you record with a company that take three or four months to release what you record because they looking for the time, for the numbers, and, 'no, this number is good for the spring, this number is good for the fall', whatever, and by the time you realize they -- When you release the number is old, everything is ...
Didn't you record a number called "Variedades"? Was it you or Tito Puente?
Yeah, well no, did you put any Bop - Bossa-novas?
